transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Call recorded via Fireflies
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Diego Marquez (Redwood Infra), Jordan Lee (BlueCrest ML), Maria Santos (BlueCrest Head of ML), Omar Rahman (BlueCrest Platform), Sanjay (BlueCrest DS)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to triage a post-quantization accuracy regression observed after switching from FP16->INT8 with mixed AWQ layerwise profile. Goals: reproduce locally, identify breadth of regression (prompt-level vs distributional), propose mitigation (fallbacks, layer exceptions, stochastic rounding), and plan on-prem/VPC microbenchmarks to validate latency/throughput impact with KV cache and batching settings.

Topics Covered:
- GPTQ vs AWQ differences and when each is preferable
- Layer selection strategies for INT8 and FP8 fallbacks
- KV cache hit behavior with prefix-heavy payloads and impact on batching
- VPC networking overhead for on-prem gateway + private control plane
- Bisect plan to find offending layer(s) causing hallucination/regression
- Rollout options: canary by user cohort, model variant fallback, automatic FP16 escape hatch

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna run through what you saw in prod after the quant roll, what we've repro'ed and then Priya will talk through a bisect plan.
[00:18] Jordan Lee: Thanks. Quick context — we moved a couple of models to INT8 AWQ on Redwood Dedicated last week and saw a noticeable drop in exact-match for our QA prompts, and some odd hallucinations on long-context prompts. Not universal, maybe 6-8% on our test set.
[00:33] Maria Santos: Yep, hit our NPS internally, so we want to understand whether this is quantization bias or something in our prompt orchestration.
[00:45] Priya Nambiar: Got it. First pass: is the regression isolated to a single checkpoint or across multiple checkpoints? Jordan?
[00:53] Jordan Lee: We applied the same quant recipe to two checkpoints derived from the same training run; both show the drop but slightly different magnitudes.
[01:05] Priya Nambiar: That hints at a layer-sensitivity issue, not a one-off corrupted weight artifact. We'll plan a layerwise bisect. Two more quick questions: are you using KV cache prefixes aggressively? I saw in the logs lots of short-prefix caching which can change effective token distributions.
[01:22] Omar Rahman: Yes, we have a lot of prefix reuse — chat-like flow, so KV cache hit rate is high. But the failing cases tend to be long-context with multiple tool call placeholders, so maybe the cache is hitting stale keys?
[01:35] Diego Marquez: Quick note, KV cache semantics change slightly with some quant kernels; compressed keys can lead to slightly different hash collisions but that's uncommon. More likely it's numerical sensitivity in late attention layers.
[01:48] Sanjay: Also seen differences when batching is increased. We bump batching to reduce cost and latencies go up slightly for tail requests, and the model sometimes truncates differently. Not sure if that's related.
[02:02] Alex Chen: Let's map that out: quant profile, batching settings, KV cache hit patterns, and prompt shapes. Priya, will you outline the bisect?
[02:10] Priya Nambiar: Sure. Step 1: reproduce locally with the customer's exact checkpoint and prompt set. Step 2: run layerwise dequantization sweep — keep all layers INT8 except X..Y and see where EM recovers. We can do block-level too, like 8-layer windows. Step 3: compare GPTQ vs AWQ artifacts and try stochastic rounding on the quantization pass. If we find certain attention layers are fragile, we propose leaving those in FP16 or FP8.
[02:36] Jordan Lee: Can you explain the GPTQ vs AWQ practical differences here? We tried GPTQ initially but saw worse perf, then AWQ gave better latency but introduced this regression.
[02:45] Priya Nambiar: In practice, GPTQ optimizes per-tensor scale ranges often yielding slightly better fidelity for some networks but at cost of bigger kernel overheads for inference. AWQ trades more aggressively, usually smaller kernels and faster memory paths. AWQ can amplify rounding bias in certain layer activation distributions, especially feed-forward dense layers with heavy skew.
[03:07] Maria Santos: So AWQ could be faster but less robust on corner-case prompts.
[03:13] Priya Nambiar: Exactly. Sometimes mixing GPTQ and AWQ by layer type helps — e.g., attention layers GPTQ, MLP layers AWQ, or leaving first/last few layers in FP16.
[03:24] Alex Chen: Any experience with FP8 as an intermediate? FP8 was mentioned in our research notes.
[03:30] Diego Marquez: FP8 can be a good middle ground; it preserves dynamic range better than naive INT8 scaling, but hardware support varies. On your dedicated infra we saw ~5-8% higher memory than INT8 but latency remains competitive. On on-prem older GPUs FP8 kernels might not be available, so fallback to mixed FP16/INT8 happens.
[03:51] Jordan Lee: Our dedicated pool is a mix of A100 and older 80GB cards — some support optimized FP8, some don't. That's probably a deployment complexity.
[03:59] Priya Nambiar: That matters for rollout strategy — you may want host-level routing to model variants depending on hardware capability. Redwood supports routing by model variant and hardware.
[04:10] Omar Rahman: Network question — if we run the private deployment behind VPC and use a gateway for on-prem, do we expect any extra latency that could interact with batching and make tail latency worse?
[04:20] Diego Marquez: There's a small added RTT for control-plane calls during model load or cache misses; for steady-state token generation the data path is optimized and that overhead is minimal. But if you have very small request sizes and aggressive batching, the added jitter can change scheduling boundaries and lead to different batch compositions — that can surface as subtle behavior changes.
[04:41] Sanjay: Interesting, so the network jitter could change which prompts are co-batched and that changes effective runtime numerics slightly?
[04:47] Priya Nambiar: It can. Especially with dynamic batching and KV cache usage; when prefix hits reduce compute we may fill batches differently and change internal RNG state ordering. Tiny changes cascade in autoregressive models.
[05:00] Jordan Lee: Okay, let's talk repro. I can share a 500-sample set where we saw regression, plus the exact checkpoint SHA.
[05:06] Alex Chen: Perfect. We'll try to reproduce on Redwood Dedicated and on a local on-prem worker to see whether the environment matters. Priya, walk us through the bisect schedule and how you'll present results.
[05:15] Priya Nambiar: We'll do a three-tier bisect: coarse (8 layer windows), fine (1 layer at a time around suspect windows), and micro (per-block or per-linear if needed). For each run we'll collect EM, BLEU-ish similarity, token-level KL divergence, and a small hallucination classifier score. We'll also capture kernel-level float traces for suspect layers. We'll present a table with per-layer delta against baseline FP16.
[05:41] Jordan Lee: How long will that take? We have a hard cadence — need to decide by next week whether to rollback.
[05:46] Priya Nambiar: Coarse sweep should be fast — a few hours on the dedicated pool for your 500-sample set. Fine sweep could take a day. Micro could be another day depending on how noisy results are. We'll prioritize quick wins like adding a last-layer FP16 exception which is usually fast to test.
[06:02] Maria Santos: If we do layer exceptions, what's the cost delta? It might increase memory and token cost.
[06:09] Diego Marquez: Leaving N layers in FP16 increases per-token compute cost slightly; if it's only last 2-3 layers the overall throughput hit is usually small (single-digit percent) but it depends on your sequence length distribution. We can quantify in the microbenchmark.
[06:23] Priya Nambiar: Also we can test stochastic rounding in quantization step which often recovers accuracy without needing FP16 exceptions. That is a parameter we can toggle in the offline quantizer.
[06:34] Sanjay: Any automated checks to catch this before rollout? We want a guardrail.
[06:38] Alex Chen: Yep — Redwood Optimize can run test prompt suites against candidate quant builds and surface worst-offender prompts and a regression score. You can gate deploys on a threshold.
[06:48] Jordan Lee: Great. A few nitpicks — in our logs I saw some weird tokenization differences between our preprocessing and Redwood's inference preproc. Could that explain hallucination differences?
[06:58] Priya Nambiar: Tokenization mismatches absolutely can affect output. Please share your tokenizer config and we will run exact-match token-level diffs.
[07:05] Jordan Lee: We'll send that.
[07:08] Maria Santos: On the ops side, if we need to run on-prem microbenchmarks simulating VPC routing, what's required from our side?
[07:16] Diego Marquez: We need a small VM with a data-plane agent and access to the model artifacts or a checkpoint. We can orchestrate a short hammer test that simulates your prefix-heavy workloads and observe latency/throughput and KV cache hit ratios. Expect 1-2 hours to set up and a few hours to run.
[07:31] Omar Rahman: We can provision that this week.
[07:34] Alex Chen: Good. Priya, mention any known gotchas with GPTQ rollbacks.
[07:38] Priya Nambiar: When rolling back to GPTQ you may gain fidelity but lose some kernel optimizations, which can increase p99 latency; so we typically do two variants: high-fidelity GPTQ for critical cohorts and AWQ for cost-sensitive. Also ensure your rollout policy in the Console can pin routes by user cohort or request metadata.
[07:56] Jordan Lee: For the bisect results we want both accuracy numbers and per-token cost estimates so we can make a business decision.
[08:04] Priya Nambiar: We'll include both.
[08:07] Alex Chen: Okay let's record explicit next steps. Jordan will share samples and tokenizer and checkpoint. Priya will run the bisect and share artifacts. Diego will stand up on-prem microbenchmark with Omar. We'll also try stochastic rounding and FP8 config where possible.
[08:23] Jordan Lee: We'll upload the dataset and checkpoint to the shared drive, link in the notes.
[08:28] Alex Chen: I'll also attach kernel logs and link to our benchmark.csv and the per-layer delta template.
[08:33] Maria Santos: Thanks everyone. A few quick questions before we wrap — if we find the regression is only in very rare prompts, could we just route those to FP16?
[08:42] Priya Nambiar: Yes — you can detect trigger prompts with a small classifier or heuristic and route them to a high-fidelity variant. That is more operationally complex but feasible.
[08:52] Sanjay: Any known examples where layerwise exceptions fixed hallucinations?
[08:56] Priya Nambiar: Yes, we've had cases where keeping the first two attention layers and last FFN in FP16 recovered QA accuracy. Those tended to be models with skewed activations in early attention and high dynamic range in last FFN.
[09:09] Jordan Lee: All right, thanks.
